data.title: Wall St Week Ahead-'Black Friday' brings consumer spending into focus for AI-rocked market
data.description:
* Anthropic IPO, solid Nvidia ( NVDA ) earnings fail to lift market

* Holiday retail sales seen up 4.2%, per Oxford Economics

* Consumer spending in focus in light of higher prices, energy costs

By Lewis Krauskopf

NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Investors will turn attention next week to the strength of consumer spending, as they hope evidence of a broadly solid economic backdrop can provide stability for a US stock market that has been shaken by unease about the AI trade.

Next week, "Black Friday" heralds the onrush of the holiday shopping season as retailers offer a wave of discounts. Investors will watch for signs of how consumersare coping with inflation, including rising energy and borrowing costs. Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of the US economy.

"If you continue to see a strong consumer, it should help to lift the economy," said Jim Baird, chief investment officer with Plante Moran Financial Advisors. "That directly contributes back to stronger corporate revenue and earnings growth, and provides a catalyst for investors that extends beyond the AI trade and to other parts of the economy."

Investors are still digesting a steep pullback in heavyweight technology and AI stocks.

This week, the blockbuster market debut from Claude creator Anthropic and a solid quarterly report from beleaguered AI chipmaker Nvidia ( NVDA ) failed to steady the stock market. Spurred by concerns about heavy financing needs and political pushback, doubts have emerged about the massive spending on data centers and other AI infrastructure that has underpinned the 4-year-old bull market.

"Markets and investors are looking at the tech sector with a lot more questions," said Paul Nolte, senior wealth adviser and market strategist at Murphy & Sylvest Wealth Management.

The Anthropic IPO offered investors their first chance to invest in a publicly traded AI lab, and the stock's performance was expected to drive broad sentiment in coming days. Anthropic's shares opened sharply higher on their first day of trading, then pared gains and closed up 17% on Thursday, while major stock indexes sank.

Dragged lower by tech stocks, the S&P 500 was last down 8% from its October 6 all-time high. The technology sector has slumped nearly 19% in that time.

A recent series of technology snafus that disrupted areas from banking to travel to email also left investors edgy heading into a US trading week that will be shortened due to the Thanksgiving holiday.

SOLID OCTOBER RETAIL SALES SETTING HOLIDAY TONE?

Weakness in stocks could threaten consumers' holiday gift-buying, if they feel less wealthy and less likely to spend.

Oxford Economics estimates that holiday retail sales will rise 4.2%, or an increase of 2.2% in volume after adjusting for inflation. That covers retail spending in November and December, excluding autos, gasoline, and bars and restaurants.

The National Retail Federation projects 182.7 million consumers plan to shop this year during the five-day Thanksgiving period that runs to "Cyber Monday", citing results from a recent survey. Black Friday is expected to be the most popular day to shop during that period. That overall number would be down slightly from 186.9 million last year, but continues the trend of elevated shopping during the holiday weekend in recent years, the NRF said.

Government data this week showed US retail sales for October increased moderately, while the core measure of such sales rose faster than expected. Retailers including Walmart ( WMT ) and Target ( TGT ) had upbeat comments or outlooks for the holiday season in their quarterly reports this week.

"The consumer is pretty healthy, and we'd like to see that continue through the end of the year," Nolte said.

COULD GASOLINE PRICES SAP SHOPPING?

Despite solid retail sales data, Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group, said he was worried "that the consumer is being impacted by higher gas prices, higher energy prices, higher food prices."

The average national price for a gallon of gasoline stood on Thursday at $3.72, according to motorists' group AAA. That is down from nearly $4.30 a month ago, but well above the $3.09 level a year ago.

As the holiday shopping season heats up, Goldman said he was watching the extent of shopping done in stores compared to online, and how much consumers are buying necessities versus discretionary items.

"If the economy exceeds expectations, earnings increase, and earnings drive stock prices," Goldman said.

Investors in the coming week also will monitor reports on inflation and consumer confidence along with an updated read on third-quarter US GDP. Quarterly results are due from Dell Technologies ( DELL ) and semiconductor company Analog Devices ( ADI ) , which could sway the AI and tech trade.

With just over a month left in 2026, the S&P 500 was on track for a year-to-date gain of nearly 5%. The index had fallen for six straight sessions as of Thursday, and this week dropped below its 200-day moving average -- a closely watched trendline -- for the first time since April.

"There is a lot to like about the fundamentals" of the market, said Mark Hackett, chief market strategist for Nationwide. "But picking bottoms is difficult when the market is so emotional."

(Reporting by Lewis Krauskopf, editing by Colin Barr and David Gregorio)

data.title: Fed's Paulson backs further rate hikes, says shared understanding beats guidance
data.description:
NEW YORK, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia President Anna Paulson said on Thursday the Fed will need to raise interest rates again because inflation is too high, while arguing that shared understanding matters more than explicit guidance on the rate outlook.

For the Fed, "understanding matters more than the specific ways we communicate," Paulson said in a speech delivered before a gathering held by the Money Marketeers of New York University.

"When we understand each other, we don't need to say as much when new data arrive," she said, adding, "You can anticipate how we'll respond, and we can act in ways that are steady and, for the most part, predictable."

Paulson's views on Fed communications come as the central bank has been overhauling how it explains its actions to the public. Under new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, the Fed has shortened its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) policy statement and has launched a special task force to weigh how the Fed should communicate its actions and views.

At the same time, Warsh has, in contrast to other recent Fed leaders, stepped almost entirely away from providing any guidance about the interest-rate outlook.

But even as Warsh has pulled back, many of his colleagues on the central bank have continued to provide regular updates on where they think interest-rate policy is heading and how the economy is faring.

Paulson said after her formal remarks that the Fed will need to raise rates again because inflation is too high in an otherwise robust economy.

"I see growth that's strengthened and I see a labor market being at full employment, and so it's clear that inflation needs to be ... the priority" of monetary policymaking right now, Paulson said after her formal remarks.

"The way we bring inflation down is by having higher rates," she said, adding that there is "more tightening to do."

Paulson also said that slow and steady rate rises rather than dramatic action give the economy time to adjust to the increase in short-term borrowing costs.

Paulson holds a vote on the FOMC this year. The committee, which sets interest rates, is widely expected to raise its target rate of between 3.75% and 4% at the meeting scheduled for December 8-9.

Paulson said in her remarks that understanding how the Fed reacts to incoming data is particularly important.

"Communication works best when it builds a shared understanding of the reaction function, and that credibility is essential, because people act on messages they trust," she said.

Paulson said an understanding of what the Fed is doing and why helped markets navigate the Fed's decision to hold rates steady in late October, after boosting them in September while signaling more hikes were in the works.

"In October, markets expected further tightening, so the pause did not leave policy behind where it needed to be," she said.

"A shared understanding of the reaction function allowed policy to move deliberately and gave people time to adjust, without the risk that a pause was mistaken for a stop."

(Reporting by Michael S. Derby in New York; Editing by Matthew Lewis and Tom Hogue)
